clue.text: Drilling large holes is really tedious

definitions.meaning: first meaning: sinking a deep shaft into the ground for water or oil
second meaning: thoroughly dull, with an informal intensifier in front

explanation.surface: Someone complains that a job drilling big holes is mind-numbingly dull.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface reads as one complaint about a dull job, but it is two meanings side by side: the trade term for drilling a well, and 'well' used as an informal 'very' before 'boring'.
explanation.definitionFit: Sinking a well shaft is literally this activity, while British slang uses 'well' as an intensifier meaning very, so the phrase also means extremely dull.

clue.text: Planet revolved rapidly we hear

indicators.note: what we hear is a spoken word, so the letters come from its sound rather than its spelling

parts.note: to whirl or spin around is to whorl, so the past tense is whorled

explanation.surface: A planet spinning fast on its axis, as reported by someone.
explanation.walkthrough: A whorl is a spiral or rapid turn; said aloud, WHORLED and WORLD are the same.
explanation.definitionFit: Our home planet is commonly called the world, so the general noun and the specific body are interchangeable here.

clue.text: City supporter idly sketches dogs

parts.note: LA is the usual abbreviation for Los Angeles
a bra is an undergarment that supports
to doodle is to draw aimlessly

explanation.surface: A fan of a city team sits drawing dogs absent-mindedly.
explanation.walkthrough: 'City supporter' looks like a football fan, but it splits into a city and a piece of underwear; 'sketches' is a verb that turns out to be a noun-like chunk.
explanation.definitionFit: Labradoodles are a popular crossbreed of Labrador retriever and poodle, so they are an example of dogs.

clue.text: Bill right to leave holiday

indicators.note: something that leaves goes away, so that letter is taken out of the word that follows

parts.note: a break is a short holiday
R is the standard abbreviation for right

explanation.surface: A proposed law giving the right to leave on holiday.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bill' reads as legislation and 'right to leave' as a legal entitlement, but the bill is a bird's, and the right is just the letter dropped from BREAK.
explanation.definitionFit: A bird's bill and its beak are the same hard mouthpart, so the two nouns are straightforward synonyms.

clue.text: Make new attempt to improve disposition of dieter

indicators.note: a disposition is an arrangement, so the following letters are set out in a new order

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Trying again to cheer up someone who is on a diet.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Disposition' pretends to mean the slimmer's mood; here it means arrangement, rearranging the six letters.
explanation.definitionFit: To re-edit a text is to go back over it a second time in order to make it better, which is a fresh attempt at improvement.

clue.text: Airmen flying over steamship narrowly avoided collision

indicators.note: in a down entry one piece sitting over another is placed above it, so it comes first
things flying about are scattered, so these letters come down in a new order

parts.note: taken as written
SS is the standard prefix for a steamship

explanation.surface: Pilots flying above a steamer only just avoid hitting it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Flying' looks literal for airmen, but it signals the rearrangement of their letters.
explanation.definitionFit: A near miss is an incident where two vessels or aircraft come close but do not actually hit each other.

clue.text: People employed to oversee party

parts.note: to direct is to supervise or oversee
Labour is a major British political party

explanation.surface: Staff hired to run a party or function.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Party' suggests a celebration, but it is the British political party. The British spelling with -OUR is needed.
explanation.definitionFit: Direct labour means workers hired by an organisation itself rather than through contractors, so it names a body of employed staff.

clue.text: On vacation, Japanese runners enjoy island

indicators.note: to vacate is to empty, so each word loses its interior and keeps only its ends

parts.note: first and last letters only
first and last letters only
first and last letters only

explanation.surface: Japanese athletes on holiday have a good time on an island.
explanation.walkthrough: 'On vacation' reads as being on holiday, but in cryptics a vacated word has its middle emptied out.
explanation.definitionFit: Jersey is the largest of the Channel Islands, lying between England and France, so it is an example of an island.

clue.text: Redesign of big car at last gave protection at the front

indicators.note: a redesign reworks the layout, so these letters are put in a new order

parts.note: taken as written

indicators.note: at last means at the end, so only the final letter of the word is kept

parts.note: the final letter of the word

explanation.surface: A restyled large car finally offered better front-end crash protection.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface is about a car's bumper or crumple zone; the protection is the body's own, shielding heart and lungs in the chest.
explanation.definitionFit: The bony cage of ribs shields the heart and lungs in the chest, on the front of the torso, so it is a guard at the front.

clue.text: Vital little Olivia is admitted to A & E

indicators.note: a patient admitted to a hospital ward goes inside it, so one piece goes within the other

parts.note: the two letters taken as written
Liv is a short form of the name Olivia

explanation.surface: A little girl called Olivia is rushed into the emergency department, her condition vital.
explanation.walkthrough: A & E (accident and emergency) is the British hospital emergency department, which makes the admission picture; here it just supplies two letters.
explanation.definitionFit: Vital in its root sense means having life, as in vital signs, so it matches being living or breathing.

clue.text: Dull poet travels west

indicators.note: in an across entry west is leftward, so the word runs from right to left

parts.note: a bard is a poet

explanation.surface: A boring poet heads off on a westward journey.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Dull poet' looks like one description, but 'Dull' is the definition and the poet is the wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: Drab describes something lacking colour or interest, which is a close synonym of dull.

clue.text: Company head shows resolve

parts.note: a firm is a business company
a ness is a headland, as in coastal place names like Sheerness

explanation.surface: A chief executive demonstrates determination.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Company head' reads as the boss, but 'head' is a headland; ness is the geographical word for one, common in British place names.
explanation.definitionFit: Resolve as a noun means determination of purpose, and steadiness of purpose is what this word expresses.

clue.text: Lovers nipping over road for wine

indicators.note: to nip is to pinch between two points, so one word grips another inside it

parts.note: beaux are boyfriends or admirers
O is the cricket abbreviation for an over
RD is the usual abbreviation for road

explanation.surface: Sweethearts pop across the road to buy a bottle of wine.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Nipping over' reads as dashing across, but 'over' is a letter and 'nipping' means pinching. An over is a set of six balls in cricket.
explanation.definitionFit: Bordeaux is the famous wine region of south-west France, and its name is used for the red and white wines produced there.

clue.text: Move to east in Tokyo city

indicators.note: east is the right-hand end of an across entry, so the named opening letters travel there

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: An instruction to relocate eastward within the Japanese capital.
explanation.walkthrough: The 'to' in the clue is both a word of the sentence and the two letters being moved, sliding from the front of TOKYO to the end.
explanation.definitionFit: Kyoto is the former imperial capital of Japan and a major Japanese city famous for its temples.

clue.text: Citadel has leaders of Kurdish architectural business excited

indicators.note: excited things are stirred up, so these letters are jumbled into a new order

parts.note: taken as written

indicators.note: leaders go in front, so each following word supplies only its opening letter

parts.note: the initial letters of the three words

explanation.surface: A fortress whose Kurdish architects are thrilled with it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Has' looks like a plain verb, but it is part of the fodder, mixed in with the three initials.
explanation.definitionFit: A kasbah is the fortified citadel of a North African town, so the walled stronghold matches the definition.

clue.text: Portion of kebabs at a yummy Malaysian meal

indicators.note: a portion is a part, so the letters come from a stretch inside the following words

parts.note: the letters run consecutively from the end of the first word into the last

explanation.surface: A helping of kebabs at a delicious Malaysian dinner.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface is a helping of food, and the helping is literally a slice of the text.
explanation.definitionFit: Satay is skewered grilled meat with peanut sauce, a well-known dish of Malaysian and Indonesian cooking.

clue.text: Rugby player Henry regularly put valuables here

definitions.note: the definition is a descriptive phrase about a place rather than a noun; the setter defines the storage cabinet by its use

parts.note: a lock is a second-row forward in rugby

indicators.note: regularly means at even intervals, so every second letter of the name is kept

parts.note: the second and fourth letters of the name

explanation.surface: A rugby player named Henry is told where to stow his valuables.
explanation.walkthrough: Henry looks like the rugby player's name, but only his even letters are used.
explanation.definitionFit: A locker is a small lockable cupboard, as in a changing room, where people store their possessions safely.

clue.text: Cross newspaper boss is returning in entrance

indicators.note: returning means going back, so the whole string runs backwards

parts.note: a rood is a cross or crucifix, as in a church's rood screen
ED is the abbreviation for editor
taken as written

explanation.surface: An angry editor coming back through the doorway.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cross' wants to be the adjective angry, describing the editor; it is the noun, a rood. The reversal covers all three pieces, not just the last.
explanation.definitionFit: A side door is a way in at the side of a building, so it is a kind of entrance.

clue.text: Dad's two assistants

indicators.note: a pair means the same thing appears twice, so one short piece is written out back to back

parts.note: PA stands for personal assistant
the second of the pair, the same abbreviation again

explanation.surface: A father who has a pair of helpers.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Dad's' looks possessive, but the 's is a link meaning 'is'. PA stands for personal assistant.
explanation.definitionFit: Papa is an affectionate or old-fashioned word for a father, a familiar synonym for dad.

clue.text: Thoroughly unpleasant legal counsel finally leaves

indicators.note: something that leaves departs, so that letter is removed from the other word

parts.note: lawful means permitted by law

indicators.note: finally means at the end, so only the closing letter of the word is used

parts.note: the final letter of the word

explanation.surface: A dreadful lawyer finally walks out.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Legal counsel' looks like one phrase for a lawyer, but 'legal' is one piece and 'counsel' gives only its last letter, which comes off the front.
explanation.definitionFit: Awful describes something very bad or dreadful, which is extreme unpleasantness.

clue.text: Hairdo for every month

parts.note: per means for each, as in miles per hour
M is the standard abbreviation for month

explanation.surface: A hairstyle redone every single month.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface suggests a monthly salon visit; 'for' is not a link here but part of the first piece.
explanation.definitionFit: A perm is a permanent wave, a chemically set curly hairstyle, so it is a type of hairdo.

clue.text: A time to go round stadium

indicators.note: going round turns something about to face the other way, so the letters run backwards

parts.note: the indefinite article in its form before a vowel
an era is a period of time

explanation.surface: It is time to do a lap of the stadium.
explanation.walkthrough: 'A time' must be read as the phrase 'an era', and the whole of it is turned round, not just the second word.
explanation.definitionFit: An arena is an enclosed venue for sport or entertainment with seating around it, much like a stadium.

clue.text: Avoid furtive look back of female

indicators.note: going back means travelling the opposite way, so the word is read from its end

parts.note: a peek is a quick, sly glance
taken as written
F is the standard abbreviation for female

explanation.surface: Don't sneak a glance at a woman's back.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Back of female' suggests the last letter of a word, a common trick; here 'back' turns the glance round and 'of' is taken literally.
explanation.definitionFit: To keep off something is to stay away from it or refrain from it, which is to avoid it.

clue.text: Additional art on the wall outside college

parts.note: extra means additional
a mural is a painting made directly on a wall

explanation.surface: More artwork painted on a wall outside a college building.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface pictures graffiti by a campus; the definition is the adjective for courses run beyond a university's own students.
explanation.definitionFit: Extramural literally means beyond the walls, and is used for university teaching offered to people who are not enrolled students.
